questions.knowledge_point: Computing a Tangent Line Approximation and Classifying it as an Underestimate or Overestimate
questions.problem: The graph of the function $y=f(x)$ passes through $(0,5)$ and is concave down on the interval $(-\pi ,\pi ).$ If ${f}^{′}(0)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},$ estimate the value of $f(\sqrt{2})$ using the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=0$ and determine whether the approximation is an underestimate or overestimate.
questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=0$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(0)+{f}^{′}(0)(x-0).\end{aligned}
$$

The function passes through the point $(0,5),$ so we have $f(0)=5.$ Also, we're told that ${f}^{′}(0)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},$ so we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =5+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(x-0) \\  & =5+\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(\sqrt{2})$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=\sqrt{2}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\sqrt{2}) & ≈L(\sqrt{2}) \\  & =5+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =5+1 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the function is concave down on the interval $(-\pi ,\pi ),$ the linear approximation $L(x)$ is above the graph near $x=0,$ and therefore we have an overestimate.

questions.problem: Let $f$ be a function such that ${f}^{′}(x)=2{e}^{2x}x(x+1)$ and $f(1)={e}^{2}.$ Use the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=1$ to estimate the value of $f(\frac{3}{4}).$
questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(1)+{f}^{′}(1)(x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $f(1)={e}^{2},$ and since ${f}^{′}(x)=2{e}^{2x}x(x+1),$ then ${f}^{′}(1)=2{e}^{2\cdot 1}\cdot 1(1+1)=4{e}^{2}.$ So, the tangent line approximation is given by

$$
L(x)={e}^{2}+4{e}^{2}(x-1).
$$

Now, we can approximate $f(\frac{3}{4})$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=\frac{3}{4}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{3}{4}) & ≈L(\frac{3}{4}) \\  & ={e}^{2}+4{e}^{2}(\frac{3}{4}-1) \\  & ={e}^{2}+4{e}^{2}(-\frac{1}{4}) \\  & ={e}^{2}-{e}^{2} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(1)+{f}^{′}(1)(x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $f(1)=3,$ and since ${f}^{′}(x)={x}^{2}(5x+1),$ we have

$$
{f}^{′}(1)=(1)^{2}(5\cdot 1+1)=6.
$$

So, the tangent line approximation is given by

$$
L(x)=3+6(x-1).
$$

Now, we can approximate $f(1.3)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=1.3.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1.3) & ≈L(1.3) \\  & =3+6(1.3-1) \\  & =3+6(0.3) \\  & =3+1.8 \\  & =4.8.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The graph of the function $y=f(x)$ passes through $(2,3)$ and is concave up on the interval $(1,4).$ If ${f}^{′}(2)=1.5,$ estimate the value of $f(1.7)$ using the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=2$ and determine whether the approximation is an underestimate or overestimate.
$\,f(1.7)≈$ {{field-1}} and the approximation is an {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=2$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(2)+{f}^{′}(2)(x-2).\end{aligned}
$$

The graph of the function passes through the point $(2,3),$ so we have $f(2)=3.$ Also, we're told that ${f}^{′}(2)=1.5.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =3+1.5(x-2) \\  & =3+1.5x-3 \\  & =1.5x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can approximate $f(1.7)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=1.7.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1.7) & ≈L(1.7) \\  & =1.5(1.7) \\  & =2.55.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the function is concave up on the interval $(1,4),$ the linear approximation $L(x)$ is below the graph near $x=2,$ and therefore we have an $\text{underestimate}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Estimating the Value of a Function at a Point Given its Derivative
questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=-1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(-1)+{f}^{′}(-1)(x+1).\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $f(-1)=2,$ and since ${f}^{′}(x)={x}^{3}-1,$ we have

$$
{f}^{′}(-1)=(-1)^{3}-1=-2.
$$

So, the tangent line approximation is given by

$$
L(x)=2-2(x+1).
$$

Now, we can approximate $f(-0.6)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=-0.6.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-0.6) & ≈L(-0.6) \\  & =2-2(-0.6+1) \\  & =2-2(0.4) \\  & =2-0.8 \\  & =1.2.\end{aligned}
$$
